extracted.intended_audience: members of the public/citizens who want to learn about and participate in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining the federal Notice-and-Comment rulemaking process so citizens can find proposed rules, submit written comments, and understand agency obligations (publication, comment periods, and agency responses). Includes guidance on using Regulations.gov and curated alert services to locate dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: When notice-and-comment applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies must follow the 'Notice and Comment' procedure (established in the Administrative Procedure Act) for creating, changing, or eliminating regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the threshold legal requirement that triggers the process — whenever an agency proposes to create, amend, or repeal a regulation, it generally must publish notice and allow public comment. The page frames this as the foundational rule governing agency rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must 'publish a "Notice of Proposed Rulemaking" in the Federal Register.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication in the Federal Register is the formal means of notifying the public about proposed regulatory changes. The NPRM should contain the proposed text, background, and instructions for submitting comments; publishing it starts the official comment process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: advance notice before effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: The process requires agencies to publish a 'Notice of Proposed Rulemaking' in the Federal Register, at least 30 days prior to the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes the timeline requirement — an agency's rule should not take effect sooner than 30 days after publication of the NPRM (i.e., commenters have time to respond and the public has notice of the impending change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period availability and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment Period — citizens typically have at least 30 days to submit written feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments are expected to be submitted in writing (electronically via the docketing portal or by other means the agency specifies). While the page states 'typically' at least 30 days, actual comment period lengths can vary by rule; commenters should check the specific NPRM for deadlines and submission instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to summarize and respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency Response — the agency publishes 'a summary of public comments it has received, along with written responses to relevant points raised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must address relevant substantive comments in their rulemaking record and explain their responses. This requirement creates a transparency and accountability standard: final rules should reflect consideration of public input and explain decisions on contested issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized electronic filing and docket access (Regulations.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov (built under the 2002 E-Government Act) is the central online portal for receiving comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Regulations.gov to find dockets, read background documents, and submit comments electronically. The page also recommends using curated alerts (e.g., Citizens Comment) and guides (e.g., Save EPA's guide) to locate relevant notices and get step-by-step help for participating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen participation rights and need for awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most citizens are unaware they can participate; 'most people do not follow the publication of Notices in the daily Federal Register' and remain unaware of their commenting rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The normative guidance is that citizens have a right to participate and should be proactive: subscribe to alerts, monitor dockets on Regulations.gov, and submit written comments during the open period. Increasing awareness is presented as an important part of effective civic engagement.
